# Posterior factorization

Let $H\in\mathbb{F}_2^{m\times n}$, let $s\in\mathbb{F}_2^m$, and suppose independent priors satisfy $\Pr(e_j=1)=p_j$. Conditioned on $He=s$, the posterior is

$$
\Pr(e\mid s)\propto
\prod_{j=1}^n p_j^{e_j}(1-p_j)^{1-e_j}
\prod_{a=1}^m
\mathbf 1\!\left[
\bigoplus_{j\in N(a)}e_j=s_a
\right].
$$

Belief propagation (BP), or the sum-product algorithm, passes local messages on the Tanner graph in order to approximate the single-coordinate marginals $\Pr(e_j\mid s)$ [@pearl1988probabilistic; @mackay2003information].

# LLR convention

Use the log-likelihood ratio

$$
L_j=\log\frac{\Pr(e_j=0)}{\Pr(e_j=1)}
=\log\frac{1-p_j}{p_j}.
$$

Positive $L_j$ favors $e_j=0$, negative $L_j$ favors $e_j=1$, and $|L_j|$ is a reliability measure. Denote variable-to-check and check-to-variable messages by $L_{j\to a}$ and $L_{a\to j}$.

::: {#def-bp-sum-product .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: binary sum-product updates

Initialize $L_{j\to a}^{(0)}=L_j$. At iteration $t$, update

$$
L_{a\to j}^{(t)}
=(-1)^{s_a},2\operatorname{atanh}
\left[
\prod_{k\in N(a)\setminus j}
\tanh\!\left(\frac{L_{k\to a}^{(t-1)}}{2}\right)
\right],
$$

followed by

$$
L_{j\to a}^{(t)}
=L_j+
\sum_{b\in N(j)\setminus a}L_{b\to j}^{(t)}.
$$

The posterior LLR estimate is

$$
L_j^{\mathrm{post},(t)}
=L_j+\sum_{a\in N(j)}L_{a\to j}^{(t)}.
$$
:::

The hard decision is $\widehat e_j=1$ exactly when $L_j^{\mathrm{post}}<0$. A decoder may stop when $H\widehat e=s$, but this test certifies syndrome consistency only. Quantum logical success requires comparing the residual operator with the stabilizer group.

## Why the check update has this form

For a parity check with target parity $s_a$, separate the even- and odd-parity contributions from all neighboring variables other than $j$. The difference-to-sum ratio of those two contributions multiplies under independent incoming messages. The identity

$$
\frac{P(0)-P(1)}{P(0)+P(1)}=\tanh(L/2)
$$

converts that product back to an LLR, while $(-1)^{s_a}$ swaps the required parity. This derivation is exact whenever incoming messages summarize disjoint evidence, as they do on a tree.

# Exactness and loopy BP

::: {#thm-bp-tree-exactness .callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem: exactness on trees

On a cycle-free factor graph, after messages have propagated across the tree, sum-product returns the exact variable marginals and exact factor marginals.
:::

On a graph with cycles, incoming messages reuse evidence after sufficiently many iterations. Loopy BP is therefore an approximation. Its fixed points are stationary points of the Bethe free energy under suitable consistency constraints [@yedidia2003understanding]. For LDPC ensembles in the large-block limit, density evolution instead tracks the distribution of messages under a local tree-likeness assumption and determines iterative-decoding thresholds [@richardson2001capacity]. These are complementary statements: a finite graph can have oscillating messages or trapping configurations even below an ensemble threshold.

# Min-sum approximation

The check update is often replaced by

$$
L_{a\to j}^{\mathrm{MS}}
=(-1)^{s_a}
\left(\prod_{k\in N(a)\setminus j}\operatorname{sgn}L_{k\to a}\right)
\min_{k\in N(a)\setminus j}|L_{k\to a}|.
$$

Min-sum overestimates magnitudes. Two common corrections are

$$
L_{a\to j}^{\mathrm{NMS}}=\alpha L_{a\to j}^{\mathrm{MS}},
\quad 0<\alpha<1,
$$

and

$$
L_{a\to j}^{\mathrm{OMS}}
=\operatorname{sgn}(L_{a\to j}^{\mathrm{MS}})
\max\{|L_{a\to j}^{\mathrm{MS}}|-\beta,0\}.
$$

The normalization $\alpha$ or offset $\beta$ is an algorithm parameter and should not be conflated with temporal damping [@chen2005reduced]. The two-smallest-magnitudes trick evaluates all outgoing min-sum messages from one check in time linear in the check degree.

# Damping and schedules

Given a newly computed message $\widetilde L^{(t)}$, damping sets

$$
L^{(t)}=(1-\gamma)\widetilde L^{(t)}+\gamma L^{(t-1)},
\qquad 0\le\gamma<1.
$$

Damping can suppress oscillations but changes neither the fixed-point equations nor the underlying factorization. Flooding schedules update all checks and then all variables; serial or layered schedules immediately reuse new messages and often converge in fewer iterations. Parameter values are code- and noise-model dependent and should be reported with benchmark results.

# Failure mechanisms in quantum LDPC codes

Quantum stabilizer matrices frequently contain many short cycles because the $X$- and $Z$-check spaces must be orthogonal. Moreover, the posterior may have symmetries generated by low-weight stabilizers. These structures produce several distinct failure modes.

## Symmetric beliefs

Suppose several low-weight errors explain the same syndrome and are related by code symmetries. Their posterior mass can split across variables so that every marginal favors zero, even though the all-zero hard decision violates the syndrome. This is a failure of bitwise marginal decisions, not evidence that no likely compatible error exists.

## Trapping and absorbing sets

Small subgraphs can support a stable incorrect fixed point under iterative decoding. Their influence is visible as an error floor at low physical error rate. Classical trapping-set theory remains relevant, although stabilizer degeneracy introduces additional symmetries [@dolecek2010analysis].

## High-weight checks

For equal incoming magnitude $L>0$ and check degree $d_c$, the sum-product output magnitude is

$$
2\operatorname{atanh}\!\left[	anh(L/2)^{d_c-1}\right].
$$

It decreases as $d_c$ grows. A violated high-weight check can therefore be too weak to overturn strong priors in early iterations.

## Degeneracy-aware versus binary BP

Running independent binary BP decoders on $H_X$ and $H_Z$ ignores correlations between Pauli components. Quantum-aware variants pass messages over the four-symbol Pauli alphabet or modify priors using stabilizer information. Even then, BP estimates local marginals; it does not automatically perform the stabilizer-coset sum required for degenerate maximum likelihood [@poulin2008iterative].

# From BP to BP+OSD

BP produces information that remains valuable when its hard decision is invalid: the posterior LLR magnitudes rank coordinates by reliability. [Ordered-statistics decoding](ordered-statistics-decoding.qmd) uses this ranking to solve the syndrome equation exactly and search a controlled list of nearby candidates. The combined method is summarized in [BP+OSD for Quantum LDPC Codes](bp-osd-decoding.qmd).

# Numerical safeguards

A robust implementation should

- clip the argument of $\operatorname{atanh}$ away from $\pm1$;
- handle zero messages with a fixed sign convention;
- separate normalization from damping;
- retain redundant checks only deliberately;
- verify $H\widehat e=s$ after every reported correction; and
- measure logical failure rather than treating syndrome validity as success.
